To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dose calculation algorithm (DCA) in the Eclipse treatment planning system (TPS) is capable of calculating accurate dose distributions for unflattened beams.
the dose calculation algorithms in the commercial treatment planning systems (TPS) are accurate for the treatment planning of photon beams with flattening filters.

advanced dose calculation algorithms (e.g., pencil beam convolution, superposition-convolution, Monte Carlo) are capable of accurately predicting dose distributions from unflattened beams, provided that the input data for these algorithms (e.g. beam profiles, beam energy spectra, beam hardening factors) are accurate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of a novel method for the calculation of dose distributions in radiation therapy.
the dosimetry of unflattened beams, with particular emphasis on Monte Carlo calculations.

the dosimetric accuracy and precision of the advanced dose calculation algorithms in the treatment planning systems (TPSs) for unflattened beam radiation therapy (RT) with photon beams, which is a new RT technique for treating deep-seated tumors with a high dose gradient.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the convolution/superposition algorithm in the Eclipse treatment planning system for the calculation of dose from unflattened photons is accurate to within a few percent.
, in general, the use of advanced dose calculation models for unflattened beams is not recommended.
the dose calculation algorithms in Eclipse, Pinnacle and RayStation are accurate for photon beams with field sizes of 10 cm or larger.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dose calculation accuracy for unflattened beams is improved when the beam is modeled as a combination of multiple photon energies.
the accuracy of the advanced dose calculation algorithms (ACAs) for unflattened photons has improved over time.
we have developed and validated a novel approach for calculating the dose from unflattened beams in radiotherapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when compared to a conventional treatment plan with flattened beams, the use of unflattened beams in IMRT plans for lung cancer can lead to significant dosimetric improvements.

, for the majority of the cases, there is a good agreement between the dose distributions calculated with the three algorithms, and the dose differences are within the recommended tolerance limits for the majority of points in the dose distributions.
, when using unflattened beams, the accuracy of dose calculations is highly dependent on the beam model used.
